text: Write a stack whose interface is the abstraction and whose array is the representation. Fill in the three blanks.
choices: Stack s = new Stack(); s.push(1); s.push(2);
explanation: Verified: it prints `2 1`. The two side-effecting expressions are worth reading slowly — `items[size++]` writes then advances, and `items[--size]` retreats then reads, which is exactly the symmetry that makes a stack work. Note that a caller sees only push and pop, so replacing the array with a linked list would change nothing they can observe. That is what makes the array a representation rather than the type.
